newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli economy seen unscathed by corruption crisis.
newsitem.headline: Israeli economy seen unscathed by corruption crisis.

text.p: Share rises on the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange on Wednesday indicated a threat to the Israeli government's stability from a corruption scandal was perceived as over for now, traders said.

"The effects of this affair on the financial market in Israel are over for the time being," said Eli Nahum of Zannex Securities. "Netanyahu won this battle...the threat to the stability of the government has vanished for now."
The benchmark Mishtanim index closed up 1.20 percent on Wednesday, the first trading day after the stock market was closed for the first two days of Passover on Monday and Tuesday.
The market is working on a reduced schedule during the week-long holiday.

On Sunday night, Israel's attorney general said there was insufficient evidence to charge Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with fraud and breach of trust in the short-lived appointment of an attorney general in January.
Police, after a three-month investigation, had recommended Netanyahu and Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi stand trial.

Netanyahu's government coalition remained intact after members who had threatened to quit decided to stay when Netanyahu and Hanegbi were not charged despite prosecutors saying there were real suspicions against them.
Traders predicted the affair would only effect the stock market if the government was seen as unstable but analysts differed over what lingering effect it would have on Israel's economy.

Members of Israel's political opposition have appealed to Israel's High Court to set aside the prosecutors' decision and charge Netanyahu and Hanegbi. Legal experts say their chances of winning are slim.

"So far there was an atmosphere of uncertainty which was the reason for drops in shares," said Avner Stepak of Meitav Brokerage Investment House, referring to a small dip in shares in the days before prosecutors issued their report.
"Since it became clear there is no real danger of the government collapsing, the trend of the market rising has continued," Stepak said. "All together there is a positive atmosphere."
Not all analysts saw so rosy a picture. In addition to the court appeals, a citizens' group is calling for a commission of inquiry into the affair.

"The...affair is not finished and the longer it drags on the worse it will be," said Pinchas Landau, economic commentator for the Jerusalem Post daily newspaper. "Its effect is that the government, which was paralysed anyway in its economic policy, is even more paralysed now."
Landau said strains in relations between Netanyahu and Finance Minister Dan Meridor could only increase since Meridor was among those who had threatened to bolt over the scandal.
Landau predicted foreign investors would conclude the Israeli government was "ineffectual and incapable of dealing with the problems at hand."
